## Conclusion

**No — current high-quality evidence does not support that coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) meaningfully improves motor symptoms or slows disease progression in Parkinson's disease.**

Early small phase II trials suggested that CoQ10 (300–1200 mg/day) might slightly slow functional decline as measured by the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) in early, untreated PD patients, generating optimism about a possible disease-modifying, mitochondria-protective effect (https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/clinical-trials/effects-coenzyme-q10-coq-parkinson-disease; https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/782965). However, these findings needed confirmation in larger trials.

That confirmation came from a large, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase III trial (published in JAMA Neurology), which tested high-dose CoQ10 (1200 mg/day and 2400 mg/day) in early PD patients. The trial was halted for futility — CoQ10 showed no benefit over placebo in slowing symptom progression or improving motor function (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/1851409). This was widely reported as CoQ10 "striking out" as a Parkinson's treatment (https://www.alzforum.org/news/research-news/coenzyme-q10-strikes-out-phase-3-parkinsons).

A more recent systematic review (2022, MDPI) examining CoQ10 in parkinsonian syndromes similarly concluded that despite biological plausibility (CoQ10's antioxidant/mitochondrial role, and lower tissue CoQ10 levels observed in some PD patients), clinical trial evidence has not demonstrated consistent or clinically meaningful benefit for movement symptoms (https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4426/12/6/975).

**Bottom line:** While CoQ10 is generally safe and well-tolerated, robust Phase III trial data show it does not improve movement symptoms or slow disease progression in Parkinson's disease. It should not be relied upon as a treatment for PD motor symptoms.
